subsystems.name: Rotor
subsystems.role: a continuous cable that circulates fast enough that its momentum, not any tower, holds the structure aloft; it also stores kinetic energy.

subsystems.name: Sheath
subsystems.role: the vacuum tube the rotor rides in, levitating it magnetically and shielding it from air drag.

subsystems.name: Ground stations and anchors
subsystems.role: two small anchor points where the loop curves down; they carry the unbalanced vertical force and house drive machinery.

subsystems.name: Payload accelerator and release
subsystems.role: accelerates a carrier magnetically along the upper sheath and releases it at altitude with near-orbital speed.

subsystems.name: Power and energy recovery
subsystems.role: spins the rotor up, supplies launch pulses, and absorbs energy back when payloads launch.

subsystems.name: Control and stability system
subsystems.role: keeps a tens-of-kilometres-long flexible structure from wobbling or drifting.

buildSteps.title: Choose the site
buildSteps.detail: The loop must run broadly east–west to gain from Earth's rotation, spanning about 2,000 km between two anchors on land or shallow sea, avoiding storm tracks.

buildSteps.title: Build the anchors
buildSteps.detail: Ground stations are constructed at both ends, with foundations sized for the downward pull of the loop and space for drive motors.

buildSteps.title: Make the rotor
buildSteps.detail: A high-strength cable with magnetic material along it is manufactured and joined into a single closed loop long enough to run the whole span and back.

buildSteps.title: Build the sheath
buildSteps.detail: Vacuum tube segments with levitation coils and motor windings are assembled along the loop route on the ground.

buildSteps.title: Load the rotor into the sheath
buildSteps.detail: The cable is threaded into the tube and the enclosure is sealed and evacuated in sections.

buildSteps.title: Spin up and lift
buildSteps.detail: The rotor is accelerated gradually; as its speed rises the loop rises off the anchors into its arch tens of kilometres high — the structure deploys itself by its own momentum.

buildSteps.title: Fit the accelerator and release system
buildSteps.detail: Accelerator windings, payload carriages and the release mechanism are installed along the upper span.

buildSteps.title: Commission
buildSteps.detail: Uncrewed payloads are launched and caught, rotor control is tuned, and the energy-recovery cycle is tested.

buildSteps.title: Scale to payloads
buildSteps.detail: Acceleration, release timing and orbital insertion are refined until commercial payloads can be delivered reliably.

prerequisites.why: the rotor needs kilotonnes of strong, magnetically levitable cable in one continuous loop; nothing like it has been made.
maglev trains demonstrate the principle, but not at kilometres per second in vacuum.
large vacuum chambers exist, but keeping a 2,000 km tube evacuated and leak-tight is unprecedented.

prerequisites.tech: Active control of very long flexible structures
prerequisites.why: the loop must resist buckling, waves and weather while carrying a payload at orbital speed.

prerequisites.tech: Megawatt-class linear motors and power electronics
prerequisites.why: these are deployed in industry and transport and would form the accelerator and drive.

pathway.milestone: a 1985 engineering concept with no funded construction programme
pathway.unlocks: a physics-consistent alternative to rockets, studied only on paper.

pathway.milestone: subscale demonstrations of vacuum maglev at kilometres per second and of long-span active damping
pathway.unlocks: evidence that the rotor and sheath can work together at all.

pathway.milestone: a short, low-altitude test loop launching small payloads suborbitally
pathway.unlocks: data on energy recovery, control and cost.

pathway.milestone: a full-length loop with a small payload capability
pathway.unlocks: very low-cost launch if the structure can be stabilised and paid for.
cheap bulk access to orbit — contingent on materials and control far beyond today's state.
